name: Dental midline correction

card.summary: Aligning the centre line of the teeth; the concept is defined, but there is no evidence on its appearance effect.

quick.overview:
The dental midline is the line between the upper or lower central incisors. If the upper and lower midlines do not match, it is called a deviation.
Correction usually refers to orthodontic alignment.
quick.mechanism: Orthodontic tooth movement shifts the arches so the midlines coincide.

lead: Dental midline correction is the adjustment of teeth, usually through orthodontic treatment, so that the line between the upper (or lower) central incisors lines up with the midline of the face or with the opposing arch. People pursue it for a more symmetrical, balanced smile: when the dental midline sits off-centre, the smile can look slightly skewed, and bringing it back to centre is one of the ways orthodontists tidy up the front of the smile. [1][2]

Each arch has its own midline, marking the contact between the central incisors. When the lower teeth shift sideways relative to the upper, the midline is described as deviated, for example a lower shift of about 2 mm to the left. [1] Case reports describe correcting midlines with differentiated orthodontic mechanics and with skeletal anchorage from mini-implants. [3][4]

Studies of how people perceive midline deviations suggest small shifts often pass unnoticed; a 2025 survey of 242 laypeople in Nablus found shifts up to 3 mm were rated acceptable and attractive.[5] Earlier studies summarised in that paper report thresholds ranging from about 1.8 mm to 4 mm depending on the study, the faces shown and the raters.[5] In looksmaxxing discussions, midline alignment is treated as one component of smile and facial symmetry.

Treatment ranges from fixed braces with elastics to clear aligners, skeletal anchorage with mini-implants and, in complex cases, jaw surgery.[4][6] No randomized trial of midline correction for appearance was located; published work consists largely of case reports and perception surveys.

chain: Braces, aligners, elastics or mini-implants shift tooth positions
Upper and lower dental midlines coincide, ideally with the facial midline
angle.text: An off-centre dental midline can make the front of the smile look asymmetric. Orthodontic correction moves the teeth so the midline sits where it should, and the person's smile reads as more balanced.

paras: The dental midline refers to the contact point between the central incisors in each arch. In the textbook ideal, with teeth of ideal size, shape and position in maximum intercuspation, it is the midsagittal line of both arches. A deviation exists when the midlines of the upper and lower arches do not coincide. [1]

In Wikipedia's illustrated example, a patient has a midline about 2 mm off to the left, with the lower jaw measured against the upper jaw and an edge-to-edge bite with Class III occlusion; the numbering diagram places the ideal midline between teeth 8 and 9 above and 24 and 25 below.[1] The article cites Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion as its source.[1]

Midline discussion often concerns the relationship between the dental midline and the facial midline, and between the upper and lower arches. The case reports available describe midline discrepancy alongside asymmetry treated with skeletal anchorage[4] and alveolar distraction in a cleft palate patient.[3]

Orthodontic treatment uses fixed braces with wires that control tooth movement in three dimensions, and rubber elastics and springs that apply additional force; removable clear aligners are an alternative. [6] Braces typically stay on for one to three years, with adjustments every four to ten weeks, followed by retainer wear because teeth can relapse. [6]

Case reports describe more specialised approaches. A 2001 report described differentiated orthodontic mechanics for midline correction. [2] A 2009 case report used a two-component mini-implant for skeletal anchorage, noting that conventional tooth-borne mechanics for asymmetry can have side effects. [4] A 2014 case report in a cleft palate patient combined alveolar distraction with midline correction. [3] Severe malocclusions can require jaw surgery. [6]

Orthodontics as a field has roots in attempts to align teeth dating to around 1000 BC. Norman Kingsley published Oral Deformities in the mid-1800s, Edward Angle created the malocclusion classification still in use and introduced the edgewise appliance in 1928, and Lawrence Andrews defined ideal occlusion in 1972 and introduced the straight-wire appliance in 1976.[6] Retainers are needed because teeth tend to relapse; over half of patients show some reversion within ten years.[6] Wikipedia says evidence for clear aligners is limited and of modest quality, and notes risks such as decalcification with poor hygiene and the use of extractions in roughly half of cases.[6]

A 2025 cross-sectional survey in Nablus asked 242 laypersons to rate smile attractiveness for upper midline deviations of 0 to 5 mm, shown as lips-only photographs and as photographs including the chin and part of the nose. Deviations up to 3 mm were rated acceptable and attractive in both sets, ratings declined at 4 and 5 mm, and adding the chin and nose did not significantly change ratings. [5]

The authors place their finding between earlier studies, which reported that shifts above 2 mm were unacceptable and that shifts up to 4 mm might go unnoticed. [5] A single small survey does not settle where the threshold lies for any given face.

The study recruited adults without dental training or orthodontic treatment (127 women and 115 men aged 20 to 49), who rated twelve photographs on a 1 to 10 scale; photographs were drawn from an earlier study.[5] Median ratings were 7 for both photo sets, gender and age had no significant effect, and about 29 percent gave the no-deviation full-face smile a score of 8. The authors listed limitations: a sample drawn from one city and smaller than the calculated target of 385, borrowed photographs and self-reported ratings.[5]

Earlier studies summarised in the paper differ: some judged discrepancies over 2 mm unacceptable, others found laypeople often failed to detect shifts up to 4 mm, Canadian laypeople accepted up to about 1.83 mm compared with 2.9 mm for Americans, and thresholds varied with face shape and rater sex.[5]

Published work consists mainly of case reports of midline correction methods, including a 2001 report on differentiated orthodontic mechanics,[2] a 2009 report using a two-component C-orthodontic mini-implant,[4] and a 2014 report of simultaneous alveolar cleft closure and midline correction with curvilinear intraoral distraction,[3] together with perception surveys.[5] No randomized trial of midline correction for appearance was located.
